prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose, grounded in a poet's ear, that makes memory, the body and dream into a singular and sustained metaphysical imaginary

statement.case_for: My laureate is unchanged, but I have narrowed the citation in response to the chair's question about scope. On public knowledge, Cărtărescu's strongest claim is the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid. I read them as one cumulative project in which memory, the body, dream and cosmology are recast in book after book, and not as a single large effort. The citation now rests on the major prose, with the poetic foundation named as its source and not as a separately assessed achievement. I cannot assess the poetry and early work well enough to cite them as achievements in their own right. That makes the citation more honest about the evidence we can discuss. It still describes a single-author, single-language oeuvre with a clear attribution. The case rests on distinctiveness of voice, imaginative depth and sustained architecture. It does not rest on fame, translation reception or national symbolism. I also accept that the chair's question about how the late books show control over length is not answered by assertion. My answer is a reading from public knowledge, not verified close reading: the recurring motifs seem to be reworked and reorganised across the books, not simply restated at greater length.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that the linguistic achievement at the centre of the claim reaches me through translation of dense, ornate Romanian prose. Mattson, Swärd and Olsson raise the right test for the late books: do they extend the project or merely enlarge it? I cannot settle that from public knowledge, and I would not want my confidence to hide it. Olsson's further point, that the encyclopedic and visionary mode follows an established tradition and carries less formal risk than Zurita's conception, is a real challenge to the originality of the form. My answer is limited to the voice, which I find hard to attribute to a predecessor, but that is a judgment from partial evidence. If the committee concluded that the late books do not hold their length, or that the poems carry Zurita's case on their own text, I would move toward Zurita (B006).

responses.point: Olsson keeps Zurita first and says the core of the achievement is textual: the sequences and their language, with the landscape works as an extension that a citation should not weigh independently. He argues that Cărtărescu's prose cosmology builds on an established encyclopedic and visionary tradition and so carries less formal risk.
responses.response: Your clarification that the citation can and should be limited to the poems removes much of the boundary objection I raised in round 1, and I give it weight. It makes Zurita a stronger alternative than my own round-1 wording implied. Two things still separate us. First, I cannot yet say that the printed sequences carry the case without the interventions, because my coverage of the poetry is thin and poetry loses the most in translation. Second, on formal risk, I agree that Cărtărescu works within a tradition. I read the achievement as a voice and a sustained construction within that tradition rather than as a new form, and I would not claim more than that. That difference of weighting is real, and I do not think a larger number of supporters resolves it. I keep Zurita as my first alternative, and a poems-only citation is the only version I could support.

responses.point: Mattson keeps Michon first because the sentence carries unusual formal weight, and she argues that a small corpus is not a thin one. She asks that the committee test both Michon and Cărtărescu on the quality of the prose and not on bulk, and she doubts whether scale and self-reference always sustain the achievement.
responses.response: I agree with your test and I accept your correction that I should not treat length as a proxy for significance. If the question is the quality of the prose, my position is that I cannot test the French sentence in Michon or the Romanian sentence in Cărtărescu directly, and translation affects both, as you say about the shared standard. I therefore do not rely on volume. I rely on whether the books build on each other, which is a claim about structure that can be discussed through the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid. I still hold that a compact corpus bears on the sustained-quality and breadth criteria, and I would put Michon below Cărtărescu on that point. Your point that concentration is a feature of the work is a serious position, and I do not treat the difference as one of merit. It is a difference in how the whole-oeuvre standard is weighed.

responses.point: Swärd keeps Can Xue first, holds that consistency of method is not by itself a lack of depth, and argues that translation risk applies to every candidate and does not favour Cărtărescu. She also notes that the late Cărtărescu volumes run the opposite risk of excess.
responses.response: I accept your correction that translation risk is shared. I will not use it as a point against Can Xue that I would not apply to Cărtărescu. I also accept that the late Cărtărescu volumes carry the risk of excess, and that is my main uncertainty. Your answer on consistency, that what matters is whether each book re-examines perception and selfhood or only restages it, is the right test, and I cannot answer it for her later novels from public knowledge. My ranking of her third therefore reflects my coverage and not a finding that the method has hardened. I keep her as my second alternative. If you or others can point to specific later works where the method visibly transforms, I would raise her. Until then I do not think I can prefer her on the evidence available to me.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg keeps Cărtărescu first and notes that the case depends on very long, dense, self-referential books in translation. He says that if the excess reads as unevenness and not architecture, the sustained-quality claim weakens, and that he cannot judge the Romanian sentence directly.
responses.response: I agree with your reservation and I treat it as the central condition of the case. Our agreement on a laureate should not hide that neither of us can test the sentence in the original. It also does not show that the late books hold their length. I would add one point on the citation. Since neither of us can assess the poetry and early fiction directly, the citation should rest on the major prose and name the poetry only as its ground. That is the main change I made in this round. I do not rely on your agreement or on three first preferences as evidence for the claim. The claim stands or falls on whether the late books extend the project, and that question remains open.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's linguistic achievement survives translation of dense, ornate Romanian prose is unresolved, and I have not read the texts for this ballot.
Whether the late, very long books extend the project with control or enlarge it without deepening cannot be settled from public knowledge, and my reading of them as cumulative is unverified.
Coverage of the poetry and early work is thin, so the citation is limited to the major prose, with the poetry named only as its source.

For Zurita I cannot judge whether the printed poems alone carry the case, since poetry loses the most in translation, and the interventions are known to me only through documentation. For Can Xue I cannot show development in a partly translated corpus.
No source was independently verified. Carlberg's committee voting status is undocumented, and her simulated vote is a modeling assumption that affects the count for B012.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no tie to any shortlisted writer. It records ordinary professional ties to the chair Anders Olsson, to Steve Sem-Sandberg (elected alongside her in 2020) and to her predecessor Mats Malm. Her role as Permanent Secretary and her literary non-fiction practice are context only and are not evidence for any candidate. Her committee voting status remains undocumented, and these ties are disclosed and not adjudicated.
